Indigenous leaders arrived at the United Nations this week — hundreds of Indigenous delegates gathering in Geneva for the 19th annual session of the UN Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples — to push back against a compounding threat to their lands, their rights, and their lives. The two forces bearing down on their communities — climate breakdown and armed conflict — are not moving on separate tracks. [As climate and conflict collide, Indigenous leaders confront overlapping crises at the UN](https://ictnews.org/news/as-climate-and-conflict-collide-indigenous-leaders-confront-overlapping-crises-at-the-un/) describes territories battered by record-breaking storms, desiccated by drought, and vanishing under rising seas — while peoples are simultaneously dying by the hundreds in wars and while defending that same ground. That convergence is not incidental. It is how collapse unfolds: upstream climate disruption amplifying every other pressure at once, bearing hardest on the communities with the least capacity to absorb them.

## A Declaration and the Distance It Has to Travel: Indigenous Land Rights

Nearly two decades ago, more than 100 countries adopted the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, a framework designed to protect the rights and lives of indigenous peoples worldwide. The ICT News reporting makes clear that the distance between that adoption and actual protection is where the current crisis is concentrated. Record-breaking storms still batter indigenous lands. Drought still desiccates them. Seas keep rising, and those territories keep vanishing. The declaration's existence has not paused any of it.

The political texture of that gap is visible in separate reporting: [Nepal's New Government's Fast Track Project Priority Sparks Conflict Over Indigenous Newar Lands in Khokana](https://www.culturalsurvival.org/news/nepals-new-governments-fast-track-project-priority-sparks-conflict-over-indigenous-newar-lands) documents Nepal's new government prioritizing infrastructure in a way that has put it in direct conflict with Indigenous Newar communities over their lands in Khokana. The structure — state development priorities pressing against indigenous territorial claims — is not a regional exception.

## Climate Is Not the Only Front

The climate threats catalogued in the ICT News report do not operate in isolation. The death toll documented in that same piece runs into the hundreds, spread across wars and acts of direct territorial defense. Government persecution compounds the picture further. All three forces — climate breakdown, armed conflict, state pressure — are running simultaneously against the same communities, not sequenced across separate timelines or distinct geographies. The overlap is not coincidental. Each pressure intensifies the others: communities defending their territories in active conflict zones are also the communities absorbing the first and worst effects of changing weather systems.

"Climate change, militarization, extractivism, and legal marginalization reinforce one another," said Binota Moy Dhamai, who is Tripura from the Chittagong Hill Tracts in Bangladesh and a former chair of EMRIP. That framing names the structural dynamic the Geneva gathering exists to address: not separate crises running in parallel, but interlocking pressures that compound each other's damage.

## What the Forum Makes Legible

Bringing these crises to the United Nations rather than to individual national capitals signals something about the scale at which indigenous leaders see this problem — and where they locate the failure of authority that shapes it. A UN forum is also a record: what was said, by whom, and when. Whether that record translates into anything material depends on whether the states that adopted the declaration treat it as a constraint on their own development priorities and security decisions.

The crises described this week did not begin at the UN, and a forum alone does not end them. What this confrontation makes legible is the distance between a framework built to protect indigenous land rights and the physical reality of those lands today — a distance that grows as climate disruption accelerates.

A new collection edited by Edward Fullbrook and Jamie Morgan, [23 Responses to Economics' Biggest-ever Question](https://rwer.wordpress.com/2026/07/14/23-responses-to-economics-biggest-ever-question/), puts the most consequential unresolved question in economic thought on the table: whether an economy organized around growth can continue within the biophysical limits of a finite planet — and what it means for the discipline if it cannot. Subtitled "Economics and the Biophysical Limits to Economic Growth," the volume's framing rests on a claim made by natural science: the global economy caused the climate crisis, and the crisis, now in an accelerating phase, threatens the economy's own existence. For a discipline that has "loosely guided the global economy's national economies" for over a century, that is not a refinement. It is a structural challenge.

## A Century of Guidance, a Question Left Unasked

Twenty-three separate responses to a single framing question, assembled in one volume, signals that Fullbrook and Morgan understand this not as a debate with a settled answer but as a live rupture in the discipline's foundations. That it is framed as the biggest-ever question economics has faced, and that it generates this density of differentiated response, reflects a shift in urgency — one driven by the crisis entering its accelerating phase.

The collection's central claim, grounded in natural science rather than economic theory, is that the relationship between growth and its biophysical consequences has reversed direction: growth caused the crisis; the crisis now constrains growth. What has changed is the insistence that economics, as the discipline that has guided the global economy for over a century, must now account for what natural science has established — rather than defer it to another field.

## The Policy Architecture Already Built on a Bet

The difficulty is that major institutional decisions have not waited for this reckoning. Green growth — the premise that economic expansion can be decoupled from resource use and made consistent with ecological stability — is not a fringe hypothesis. [Green growth](https://unevenearth.org/2022/10/green-growth/) by Winne van Woerden for Uneven Earth documents it as the governing assumption embedded in the European Green Deal, the Paris Agreement, IPCC reports, and the US Inflation Reduction Act, promoted by leading multilateral organizations and treated as common sense across national and international policymaking.

The institutional bet embedded in those frameworks is that the answer to the collection's central question is yes — growth can continue, cleanly enough, within biophysical limits. If the 23 responses suggest otherwise, the implications don't settle in academic journals. They land in every policy instrument that has already staked its architecture on decoupling working at the required scale.

## Growth Mania Beyond the Material Economy

The logic the collection scrutinizes is not confined to resource extraction. [Growth mania is fueling dangerous advances in AI – and its existential risks](https://www.resilience.org/stories/2026-07-09/growth-mania-is-fueling-dangerous-advances-in-ai-and-its-existential-risks/), published in Resilience, argues that AI risk represents "the apex of growth mania" — decisions made by a small number of tech elites without the consent or interests of the broader population in mind, and potentially resulting in humanity being replaced as Earth's most intelligent species. Whether the same discipline that has guided the global economy for over a century is equipped to account for that scale of consequence is not a question the current volume takes on.

## What 23 Responses Open

What the format makes visible is that the question is now being engaged at scale — that biophysical limits have generated enough serious response to constitute a volume of 23 differentiated voices, not a pamphlet from the ecological economics margin.

Every growth projection, every policy framework, every national economic plan runs on assumptions — stated or not — about what physical systems can sustain. The collection asks whether those assumptions hold.

Green growth is not simply an optimistic reading of the data. It rests on a specific intellectual foundation: an ecomodernist belief in technological progress holding that there are no limits to growth because there are no limits to human ingenuity. From this premise, the limits-to-growth tradition represents not a scientific constraint to be accommodated but a failure of imagination to be overcome. Innovation, efficiency, and circular-economy design will, in theory, allow economic output to expand indefinitely while the ecological costs of that expansion fall toward zero — a process the green growth framework calls decoupling.

Van Woerden's analysis for Uneven Earth argues that this foundation is dangerously misguided, and that the decoupling concept on which green growth's credibility depends does not hold up to scrutiny. If decoupling is not achievable at the scale and pace that the current policy architecture requires, then every framework premised on it — every Green Deal, every Paris alignment, every climate instrument that assumes growth and ecological stability are compatible — has been built on an assumption the evidence does not support.

The stakes of that evidentiary question are not symmetrical. A collection confirming that decoupling is feasible would validate the direction multilateral institutions have already chosen. A collection arguing otherwise is not merely an academic critique; it is a challenge to the legitimacy of the entire policy generation that the green growth consensus produced.

The Fullbrook and Morgan volume arrived this month, and its 23 responses represent the fuller substance that the collection's framing only introduces. What the framing already establishes is that the volume proceeds from the premise that mainstream economics has not adequately grappled with biophysical limits — that a discipline which guided the global economy through a century of expansion is confronting, in the accelerating climate crisis, the consequence of that guidance.

The green growth apparatus documented by van Woerden is the discipline's current answer: growth can continue, technology will provide, decoupling will scale. The 23 responses in the Fullbrook and Morgan collection engage that answer formally and in detail. The significance of the volume does not depend on which view ultimately prevails. It depends on the fact that the question is now being asked — systematically, by 23 contributors, in a dedicated collection — at the moment when the climate crisis has removed the option of treating it as merely theoretical.

Woodside Energy has spent years embedding AI into the operational core of its industrial systems—not as a productivity interface, but as what [Building the foundation for an autonomous enterprise](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/07/02/1138433/building-the-foundation-for-an-autonomous-enterprise/) describes as a "core operating layer." The company's trajectory predates the generative AI wave: before enterprise copilots or large language models, Woodside was building predictive analytics, optimization systems, and machine learning tools across its operations. That sequence matters, because the energy sector's path into AI was shaped by constraints—physical infrastructure, operational continuity, safety—that consumer-facing AI never had to meet.

## Before the chatbot era

The energy sector's relationship with AI began not with conversation but with prediction. Woodside's adoption, as described in a profile at MIT Technology Review, started with tools designed for a sector defined by "sprawling industrial systems and constant stream of operational data." Andrew Melouney, Woodside's vice president for digital, is quoted in the profile describing those data volumes as creating "really clear, quite high-value use cases." Predictive analytics in this context means something different from what the term typically suggests in enterprise software: it means anticipating system-level failures, optimizing operational yields, and managing infrastructure where physical continuity is the baseline requirement.

That grounding in physical consequence distinguishes industrial AI adoption from most of what the public associates with the technology. The entry point wasn't a model that writes emails; it was a set of machine learning systems engineered to keep high-stakes physical infrastructure running within safe parameters.

## Why energy infrastructure draws the analysis

Energy is not just another sector to observe for AI diffusion. Data is continuous, infrastructure is capital-intensive and geographically fixed, and the cost of a wrong output is measured in more than money. The profile frames Woodside's experience as offering "a glimpse into what that future could look like"—the future where AI functions not as a discrete application but as an ambient operating condition.

The distinction the source draws—between AI as consumer tool and AI as industrial layer—maps onto a genuine asymmetry in consequence. A miscalibrated optimization system in an industrial energy operation carries a category of risk that a malfunctioning productivity app does not.

## Who absorbs the infrastructure costs

What Woodside builds at this depth has a price that doesn't stay with the company that built it. [AI vendors have found someone to pay their infrastructure bills: You](https://www.theregister.com/software/2026/07/16/ai-vendors-have-found-someone-to-pay-their-infrastructure-bills-you/5273712) reports Forrester's finding that customers should brace for bigger software bills next year as vendors raise prices and add usage charges to pass their AI costs downstream. In a survey of more than 2,600 business and technology decision-makers, Forrester found software budgets expected to rise as Anthropic, OpenAI, and GitHub shift services from flat-rate subscriptions toward usage-based billing; Microsoft, cited separately by Forrester, launched a premium E7 license bundling M365 Copilot and Agent 365 into a higher-cost tier.

For an energy company running AI as a core operating layer rather than a discrete application, usage-based billing is a structurally different exposure than it is for an office that runs Copilot to summarize meetings. The volume of inference required to continuously monitor industrial systems at this scale is not the same category of use.

## What this model opens onto

The question Woodside's trajectory makes visible is what happens to operational continuity when the AI layer becomes load-bearing. A company that has spent years embedding machine learning into its core processes is not merely using AI—it is depending on it, in a sector where safety and physical continuity are, by the source account, paramount.

[The risk of weather data sabotage is rising](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/07/17/1140622/weather-data-sabotage/) separately notes that utilities use weather predictions to decide where to build solar and wind farms and how to price wholesale electricity, and that those forecasts are now exposed to growing sabotage risk as prediction markets create financial incentives to manipulate weather data. The Woodside model extends that logic further inward: AI not as an input to a decision, but as a continuous condition of operation itself.

The unresolved question the sector's early adoption leaves open is not whether AI infrastructure in energy operations could be re-priced or interrupted, but what operational continuity looks like for a company that has built its foundation on it if that happens.

After seven years during which the original GitHub repository sat frozen at its last commit, NextBSD has returned to active development—under new management, with a new repository separate from the original, and the same founding purpose: porting Apple's open-source Darwin code into the FreeBSD ecosystem. [The Register's FOSS desk reported the revival on July 18, 2026.](https://www.theregister.com/os-platforms/2026/07/18/nextbsd-returns-to-dollop-apple-source-on-freebsd/5273788)

NextBSD was started in 2015 by Jordan Hubbard, a co-founder of FreeBSD. The plan from the beginning was to port components of Apple's Darwin OS to FreeBSD. Darwin is the Unix foundation on which macOS and Apple's other operating systems are built; it is open source, with its code available directly from GitHub. Bridging that codebase into FreeBSD required sustained porting effort—work that exists only as long as someone is actively doing it.

## NextBSD Returns: Apple Darwin Source Porting Under New FreeBSD Stewardship

The developer who revived the project is Joe Maloney, known on GitHub as pkgdemon. Maloney is already recognized in BSD circles: he built the Gershwin desktop environment for GhostBSD, which The Register previously covered. Shortly after that coverage, Maloney approached the NextBSD maintainers and asked if he could take over the project. He had a relatively minor role in the original—his commits are visible in the project's history—and the maintainers agreed.

The new GitHub repository is distinct from the archived original, which remains accessible with its history intact. The revived project also includes a project history page crediting the contributors behind the original effort, including the work Hubbard established when he founded the project in 2015.

## What Apple Source Integration on FreeBSD Actually Requires

NextBSD's specific work is integrating Apple's open-source Darwin components into FreeBSD. This does not happen automatically: it requires deliberate porting effort each time Apple releases relevant Darwin code. Darwin's being open source makes the code available, but availability is not the same as accessibility across ecosystems. The porting work is what keeps Darwin components circulating in FreeBSD rather than remaining only where Apple's own infrastructure uses them.

The seven-year gap in the original repository's commit history is the visible record of what this work looks like when its maintainer steps back. The project did not close; the last commits simply stopped accumulating, and the gap persisted.

## FreeBSD Infrastructure Fragility and the Seven-Year Gap in Apple Source Coverage

From a systems perspective, the dormancy and revival of NextBSD is a case study in how open-source infrastructure projects that bridge major platform codebases—Darwin to FreeBSD, in this instance—depend on continued individual contribution for their continued existence. A seven-year gap in the commit history of an infrastructure bridging project is not merely a record of a pause; it is a record of an absence in the flow of Apple's Darwin code into the FreeBSD ecosystem. The porting work is a dependency, and like other infrastructure dependencies, its status is not fully visible until the maintenance stops.

Maloney's revival restarts the porting work, and the new project history page acknowledges the prior contributors. Whether the revived NextBSD builds a contributor base broad enough to reduce dependency on any single person's continued involvement is a question the new repository's commit history has only begun to answer.

## Abstract

Clickbait is best understood not as “bad headlines,” but as a **packaging technology for attention**. It converts uncertainty, emotion, identity, and platform visibility into clicks, views, comments, shares, ad impressions, affiliate conversions, or ranking signals. Its defining problem is **warrant failure**: the headline, thumbnail, preview card, or prompt makes a promise that the destination content does not adequately justify. Clickbait can appear in professional newsrooms, content farms, MFA sites, YouTube thumbnails, TikTok captions, Google Discover cards, affiliate “best-of” posts, AI-generated feeds, and disinformation-for-profit operations. It is a rhetorical form, a labor regime, and an infrastructure effect.

The central claim of this memo is that clickbait packages attention by creating **epistemic debt**: it borrows the reader’s cognitive effort in advance, promising a future payoff of knowledge, affect, recognition, outrage, shame, fear, or desire. The debt is paid when the content delivers a proportionate answer; it defaults when the package withholds, exaggerates, misdirects, or mismatches the article, image, video, or product page.

| **Content farm** | Publishing organization or network | High-volume production optimized for traffic/search | Ads, affiliates, syndication | It is an organizational model; it may use clickbait but need not always. |
| **Content mill** | Labor arrangement | Piece-rate, ghostwritten, templated writing under speed/SEO pressure | Client fees, agency margins | It names labor conditions, not just content quality. |
